title: Why things always shift on their own until they stop changing
phenomenon: A cup of hot water left standing: warm after ten minutes, room temperature after an hour. Nobody touches it.
invariant: The fraction by which it deviates from equilibrium shrinks over time with the same time constant. Half-life = τ·ln2, independent of how large the deviation is.
force_invariant: The key is not that it is cooling, but that the closer it gets to room temperature, the slower it cools. The first minute drops far more degrees than the tenth. One measurement is enough to see this — so it cannot be a coincidence. For a deviation to shrink in proportion to itself, the only possible shape is exponential decay.
check_yourself: Same cup of water: going from 90℃ down to 80℃ takes 3 minutes; how many minutes to go from 50℃ to 40℃? (Answer: still 3 minutes — because what shrinks is the fraction of the deviation from room temperature. That is why we use half-life instead of how many degrees it dropped.)
entry_question: Why does hot water cool down on its own? I never touched it.
transfer: A room's temperature approaching the ambient temperature
Debt repaid at a fixed proportion
boundary: When the temperature difference is too large, heat transfer turns nonlinear (radiation goes as T⁴); when there is an obvious temperature gradient inside the object, the very notion of one single temperature fails first; when the parameters themselves change with the state, τ is no longer constant.
reality_meaning: Wherever something is pulled back toward a line, it has this same shape: body temperature, blood sugar, inventory, emotional intensity, wound healing. When you see a quantity falling back, first ask what its time constant is — that one question works across industries.
game_instance: Resource depletion / energy drain / stamina recovery; difficulty adaptation falling back to a baseline

title: Money does not appear out of nowhere, so where does it go
phenomenon: A bathtub filling at one end and draining at the other; the water level may rise, stay level, or fall. All three are possible.
invariant: With no sources or sinks, the total is strictly conserved: d(∫ρ)/dt = 0. To say there is less, you must point to where it went.
force_invariant: The water level does not care how much flows in or how much flows out; it cares only about the difference between the two. And once you write that difference down, you find that without spelling out sources and sinks, any claim of conservation is empty words — which is exactly where most muddled accounts come from.
operator: ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = S    (continuity equation; S is the source/sink)
check_yourself: A team's headcount did not change this week, yet someone says there are fewer people — what must be added for that sentence to hold? (Answer: you must add where they went. Otherwise it is not a checkable statement.)
entry_question: Why does the water level rise? I have been draining it the whole time.
transfer: Traffic conservation (jam waves travel backward, not forward)
The flow of energy through a system
boundary: The boundary must be defined first. An open system is wrong by definition if S is omitted. Some quantities look conserved only because the observation window is too short (for example, water that leaks out as vapor being left out of the count).
reality_meaning: This is the antidote to every muddled account: when someone says it decreased or it increased, first ask where the source is and where the sink is. Personal finances, project hours, and attention all apply.
game_instance: The three ledgers of resource output / consumption / inventory; Mario's coins, lives, and time

title: Why some things start out unremarkable and later cannot be stopped
phenomenon: A snowball picks up a layer per roll, and the next roll picks up more. Rumors work the same way: one person tells ten, and those ten each tell ten.
invariant: Doubling time is constant: t₂ = ln2/k. No matter how big it is now, doubling takes the same time.
force_invariant: The key is in proportion. It is not a fixed amount added every second, but **however much there already is, it grows again in proportion to that amount**. These two growth shapes are completely different: adding a fixed amount is a straight line, growing in proportion is exponential, and the difference between them is nearly invisible in the first few rounds — which is exactly what makes it dangerous.
check_yourself: An account has 100 people on day 1 and 1,000 on day 7. Roughly how many on day 14? (Answer: about 10,000 — the doubling period is about 2.3 days. If you assumed about 150 people a day, you would predict roughly 2,000, off by 5×.)
entry_question: Why does a snowball get bigger the more it rolls? Anyone who rolled one as a kid knows it does, but why?
boundary: It holds only while resources are unlimited. Once it hits a ceiling it becomes saturated (logistic) and the curve turns into an S. Most exponential growth in reality is a brief phase before hitting the ceiling.
reality_meaning: To judge whether something will run away, you need only one set of numbers: what k is, how long the doubling time is, and where the ceiling is. Once those three numbers are stated, whether it will blow up stops being an emotional question.
game_instance: Ball speed ramping up; Space Invaders speeding up overall as enemy ships thin out; difficulty ramp curves

title: Why walking with a full cup of water is steadier
phenomenon: A thermostat: on when it is cold, off when it is hot. Body temperature is also pulled back during a fever. Every small step you take while walking corrects the sway of the previous one.
invariant: Disturbances are suppressed. Three regimes are separated by the damping ratio ζ: overdamped (slow but no overshoot), critically damped (fastest without overshoot), underdamped (fast but sways back and forth).
force_invariant: Correction cannot rely on trying hard alone. Push too hard and you overshoot, so it sways back and forth; push too lightly and it never comes back. So **the speed of correction and the amount of overshoot must match** — which explains why being extra careful actually spills the water: a slow response leaves every correction lagging behind the tilt.
operator: dx/dt = k·(x* − x) − c·ẋ    or in second-order form  ẍ + 2ζω₀ẋ + ω₀²x = 0
check_yourself: Why do many self-regulating systems start oscillating on their own? (Answer: the feedback has delay. The corrective action arrives too late, so the correction chases a state that is already past, and it becomes oscillation — see the oscillation at depth 1.)
entry_question: Walking with a full cup of water, the more careful I am the more I spill, while quick small steps do not spill. Why?
transfer: Physiological homeostasis (body temperature, blood sugar, blood pressure)
boundary: Excessive gain or excessive delay turns damping into oscillation. When nonlinearity is too strong, the number damping ratio itself is no longer defined.
reality_meaning: Every problem of keeping something that drifts on its own under control is this same problem: tune the gain, tune the delay. Knowing what ζ is tells you why both reacting too fast and reacting too slow ruin things.
game_instance: Difficulty adaptation; matching player intensity; balance tuning
